UNSW operates handle.unsw.edu.au as a separate CNRI Handle-System redirector in front of UNSWorks; it 302-redirects to the unsworks.unsw.edu.au item page but is a distinct hostname that never appears in .dspace7_hosts(). dspace7_links() checks three paths: (1) real hyperlink hrefs matching a known host -- fails, handle.unsw.edu.au isn't in the list; (2) a bare-text mention of a known host string -- fails, same reason, the text only contains "handle.unsw.edu.au", never "unsworks.unsw.edu.au"; (3) a bare DOI-shaped string ("10.xxxx/yyyy") resolved live and checked against the known-host list -- also fails, because the citation in the paper's text is a Handle-resolver URL with no "10." DOI prefix anywhere in it (the item's real DOI, 10.26190/5e1ce7350483e, only appears on the landing page itself, never in the citing paper's text). So all three of dspace7_links()'s detection paths miss this specific citation even though the underlying repository (unsworks.unsw.edu.au, DSpace 7) is fully supported. This is a configuration gap, not a missing platform or a code bug: the fix would be adding "handle.unsw.edu.au" (or a generic handle.* / hdl.handle.net resolver pattern) to the host recognition logic, analogous to how issue #435 already added live DOI-redirect resolution for the no-host-string-at-all case.

manual_why_metacheck_misses_it: metacheck fully supports Figshare and even has explicit, dedicated support for exactly this host and DOI prefix: R/archive-figshare.R's .figshare_vanity_hosts() lists "smithsonian.figshare.com" by name (line 97), and .figshare_doi_prefix_hosts() maps DOI prefix "10.25573" to "smithsonian.figshare.com" (line 136). The citation text is also cleanly extractable with no garbling. The actual bug is in ID-type resolution: the cited DOI, https://doi.org/10.25573/data.c.5073065.v1, is a Figshare COLLECTION DOI (identifiable by the literal ".c." segment after the DOI prefix, the same marker .figshare_collection_id() uses for the generic 10.6084/m9.figshare.c.<id> case), but .figshare_id()'s institutional-prefix pattern (archive-figshare.R lines 327-344) does not exclude or recognize this ".c." collection marker for institutional prefixes -- it simply strips any non-digit-containing sub-segment and returns the trailing digits, "5073065", as if it were an ARTICLE id. I confirmed this live: devtools::load_all() then .figshare_id(url) returns "5073065", but .figshare_collection_id(url) returns NA (its own pattern only checks the literal 10.6084 prefix, not institutional ones like 10.25573, per the comment at lines 460-463 of the same file: "Only the literal 10.6084 prefix is checked here... no institutional-collection-DOI citation has been found yet"). Because figshare_info() checks ids$figshare_id first and only falls through to collection-expansion logic when figshare_id is NA (line 591: "unresolved <- is.na(ids$figshare_id)"), it never tries the collection path for this URL -- it instead calls GET https://api.figshare.com/v2/articles/5073065 directly, which I confirmed live returns HTTP 404 (while GET https://api.figshare.com/v2/collections/5073065 returns HTTP 200). Running figshare_info() on this exact URL in the live package reproduces the failure: it returns a row with error = "unfound" and a warning "5073065 could not be found on api.figshare.com". This directly contradicts the payload's metacheck_any_detector_hit = true for this paper: the one link actually cited in the text is not resolvable by the current code, because institutional-prefix DOIs for Figshare collections are not yet recognized as collections the way bare 10.6084/m9.figshare.c.<id> DOIs are.

This explains why metacheck_any_detector_hit is true: the platform/host-level detection succeeds. There is a secondary, narrower limitation worth noting for completeness: the internal helper .dataone_pid() (lines 163-194), which extracts the specific persistent identifier used to query the live DataONE API for file-level verification, only has regex branches for 'doi:10.x/...' and bare DOI forms -- it has no branch matching a bare 'urn:uuid:<uuid>' citation PID (that pattern, in dash form 'urn-uuid-<uuid>', is only handled elsewhere at line 443 for parsing file identifiers already returned by the API, not for extracting the top-level citation's own PID). manual_why_metacheck_misses_it: Metacheck has a full, working Zenodo detector (R/archive-zenodo.R), and its design is explicitly built to catch bare DOI citations of the exact form "10.5281/zenodo.NNNNNNN" with or without a URL scheme or doi.org prefix (see the regex and comment at R/archive-zenodo.R lines 5 and 28: "10.5281/zenodo.1234567" is routinely cited without any URL scheme at all"). The gap here is not a missing platform but a text-extraction corruption: in the extracted full_text, the citation reads "Zenodo, https://doi.org/10.5281/ zenodo.3756781" with a literal space inserted between "10.5281/" and "zenodo.3756781" (almost certainly a PDF line-wrap artifact from GROBID/PDF-to-text conversion at a hyphenation or column break). Metacheck's R/text-extractors.R extract_urls() function, which is the upstream source of link candidates that archive-zenodo.R and other archive-*.R detectors work from, uses a \b-bounded regex requiring a contiguous domain-like token ([\w.-]+\.[a-z]{2,}) with no internal whitespace. That regex matches "https://doi.org/10.5281/" and "zenodo.3756781" only as two separate, incomplete fragments across the inserted space, neither of which satisfies the Zenodo-ID pattern (10\.5281/zenodo\.[0-9]+) that archive-zenodo.R looks for. The result is that no valid Zenodo candidate URL is ever produced for the detector to test, which is consistent with metacheck_any_detector_hit being false even though the paper does cite a fully public, CC-BY-4.0, live Zenodo dataset with three files, and even though Zenodo is a fully supported platform. This is a text-extraction/garbling problem (a split DOI token), not a missing detector and not a dead repository.

manual_why_metacheck_misses_it: Zenodo is a fully supported platform in metacheck (R/archive-zenodo.R, zenodo_links()). That function already implements a deliberate two-tier search: real hyperlinks from the paper's url table, plus a body-text fallback regex for bare DOIs like "10.5281/zenodo.NNNNNNN" that appear without a hyperlink. The problem for this specific paper is that the fallback regex is run through text_search(paper, zen_bare_regex, return = "match", perl = TRUE) without passing include_refs = TRUE, and text_search() defaults to include_refs = FALSE, which explicitly filters out any text row whose section_type is "references" (see text_search.R, the `section_filter <- !text$section_type %in% "references"` line, used whenever include_refs is not set to TRUE). In this paper, the inline data-availability sentence is a bare author-year citation with no DOI or URL at all ("The Paris 12 dataset is available on Zenodo (Machon, 2020)."; similarly for the code, "available on Zenodo (Louvet, 2020), as well as on a GitHub repository"), and the only place the actual resolvable Zenodo DOIs (10.5281/zenodo.3770339 and 10.5281/zenodo.4314518) appear anywhere in the extracted text is inside the References section's bibliography entries. Since zenodo_links() never searches the references section for its bare-DOI fallback, it finds no hyperlink and no in-body bare DOI, so it returns zero Zenodo URLs for this paper even though both repositories are live, public Zenodo records with files. This is not a missing backend (Zenodo is fully implemented) and not a garbled DOI (the DOIs are intact and correctly formatted) -- it is a configuration/search-scope gap in how the existing Zenodo detector decides which part of the document to scan for bare identifiers, which this specific paper's citation style (name-year in text, DOI only in the reference list) exposes.
